effect_mechanism: Restoring water to a degraded wetland strongly increases biodiversity. Reinstating hydrology on a degraded wetland puts back standing water and saturated soil, and the gain is measured against that degraded starting point. How degraded that point is comes from a review of agricultural use of wetlands, restating the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment: natural wetlands reclaimed by drainage and land amelioration have lost much of their original character, leading to reduced biodiversity and reduced performance of functions other than crop productivity (ev_biodiversity_outcome_verh09_5). That unit describes what reclaiming an existing wetland cost, not a restoration result; it enters this family row through the existing-wetland home-family route, as a statement of the degraded starting point rather than a measured restoration outcome. Restoring degraded wetlands enhanced biodiversity overall and the diversity of vertebrates, vascular plants and terrestrial and aquatic invertebrates (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_3). The mobile parts of the system return soonest: vertebrate assemblages reached reference structural values within a few years (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_6), and riverine and tidal wetlands kept connected by natural flow variation recovered biogeochemical function and biological structure after 20 and 30 years respectively (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_9). Project cases show the same fast early response. After the first test flooding of the restored Belene Island marshes, park reports cited by the World Bank record fish species rising from 2 to 10 within 2 months and ferruginous duck nesting pairs from 5 to 50 (ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_1); a project-supported inventory found flora and fauna beginning to regenerate after the Lapusna wetland in Moldova was restored (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mdicr_2). Reconnecting floodplains by setting levees back works the same way: a critical review of levee alteration (Knox et al.) reports reduced flood stages and improved biodiversity after a setback on the Missouri River in Iowa (Smith et al.) (ev_biodiversity_outcome_knox22_1) and a setback on the Elbe in Germany was followed by newly established floodplain forest and excavated shallow water bodies, with the documented return of many waterfowl and other bird species and a diversity of habitat types (Serra-Llobet et al.) (ev_biodiversity_outcome_serra22_2). On California's unregulated Cosumnes River, partial levee removal and setback reconnected the river to its floodplain, and the renewed flooding diversified flow and geomorphology, promoted riparian vegetation establishment and supported positive responses from native fish and the aquatic ecosystem (ev_biodiversity_outcome_serra22_5). A review of floodplain wetland restoration studies finds the same direction in how projects report themselves: most published studies deemed their restoration activities successful or partially successful, irrespective of the restoration activity performed (ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_1). The Lao and Sierra Leone units come from protecting existing wetlands rather than restoring them: in Lao PDR, designating fishery conservation zones was followed by an increase in native fish populations and more fish for local consumption (ev_wgy_lao_3), and at Sierra Leone's Mamunta Mayosso sanctuary positive changes in biodiversity conservation are confirmed after cattle settlements were banned (ev_biodiversity_outcome_wcpsl_1).
conditionality: A restored wetland that falls short of an intact one is a recovery note, not harm, and it is kept apart from the gain above. The slow parts lag: plant assemblages took decades to converge statistically with reference sites and their absolute structural values remained below reference even 100 years after restoration, with biological structure and biogeochemical functioning still lower than reference (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_7, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_1), while inland depressional wetlands fed only by precipitation or groundwater had not recovered to reference conditions decades after restoration (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_8). The global syntheses disagree on whether that shortfall persists, since biodiversity in restored wetlands did not significantly differ from that in natural wetlands (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_2). Not every group responds: macroinvertebrate diversity showed no significant effect (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_4), and a cited North American case found that restoring individual wetlands did not bring back the Topeka Shiner, a small fish; the authors argue species moving between wetlands need restoration across many wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_3]. The project units are weaker than their numbers suggest. The Bulgarian counts are park reports taken within months of the first flooding (ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_2), and the Moldovan result is direction only (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mdicr_2). The Missouri entry is a second-hand table row, direction only (ev_biodiversity_outcome_knox22_1). The Elbe and Cosumnes findings are case studies with a before/after framing and no control site, and the Elbe bird counts are project-success evaluations cited without a named underlying study (ev_biodiversity_outcome_serra22_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_serra22_5). The floodplain review is a vote count of authors' own declared success against indicators they chose, not a measured effect against a baseline, and its authors warn that unsuccessful outcomes are likely under-reported (ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_1); it also relays a before-and-after study in which hydrological restoration of inundation levels failed to restore invertebrate food sources for birds, likely because of vague aims and predictions of what the target species required (ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_2). The Sierra Leone claim is an evaluator's assertion about a bundle of grazing by-laws, boundary demarcation and co-management, and it depended on the exit of all Fula settlements and their cattle, a livelihood cost the biodiversity gain does not show (ev_biodiversity_outcome_wcpsl_1). The Lao result rests on project fish-monitoring records inside protected zones (ev_wgy_lao_3). The comparisons against intact reference sites (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_6, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_7, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_8, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_9) are held out of the class for that reason: they measure how far recovery has to go, not what restoration adds over the degraded starting point.

effect_mechanism: Wetland management moderately increases carbon storage. Raising the water table on drained peat stops the stored carbon from rotting away, so carbon dioxide losses fall, even though methane rises. Rewetting drained farmland peat in Germany is estimated to save 20 to 35 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per hectare a year [ev_wet_carbon_meye26_1], and each 10 cm the water table is raised cuts net warming by at least 3 tonnes per hectare a year [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_1]. IPCC guidance adds that rewetting cuts waterborne carbon losses (a median 36% in the studies it collated) and that nitrous oxide falls practically to zero once the water table is within 20 cm of the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc13wl_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc13wl_3]. Restored forested wetlands on former US farmland were modelled to store 15.8 to 92.4 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per hectare every five years [ev_carbon_sequestration_jenk10_1], and in Canada active moss reintroduction restored carbon uptake on extracted peat [ev_carbon_sequestration_unepgpa22_2]. Field studies confirm that blocking ditches and canals raises the water table [ev_water_table_depth_hold04_1, ev_water_table_depth_page09_1, ev_water_table_depth_wils11db_1]. On burned peat in South Sumatra, planted native trees took up 11.3 tonnes of CO2 per hectare a year (Shorea balangeran) and 12.4 tonnes (Dyera polyphylla) in their wood [ev_wet_carbon_budi20_1, ev_wet_carbon_budi20_2]. Reviews of Indonesian peat projects report canal blocks raising the water table: by about 60 cm in the dry season 100 m from a block in Riau, by 70 cm within 170 m of a block at Sungai Tohor, and by a metre over 2420 ha where communities built 12 blocks [ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_2, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_4, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_3].
conditionality: The class is moderate because the size rests on modelled results. Methane is the trade-off: where water stands above the peat surface, methane warming can outweigh the carbon dioxide saved for years [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_4], and restored wetlands can warm the climate for their first years to decades, with the switch to net cooling estimated at 57 to 299 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_4]. A meta-analysis found methane up 122.3% after restoration, with total emissions no higher than before [ev_carbon_sequestration_xu25_3]. Partial rewetting slows but does not stop peat loss [ev_carbon_sequestration_unepgpa22_4]. In a Kalimantan simulation, raising water levels gave only a small, not significant fall in carbon dioxide [ev_carbon_sequestration_page09_2], and planting on rewetted tropical peat has failed: seedlings did no better beside a dammed canal, and aerial seeding survived at about 2% [ev_establishment_survival_page09_6, ev_establishment_survival_pusp21_4]. Most evidence is temperate, boreal and high-income, and the benefit goes to the climate, not to the farmer. The South Sumatra tree figures count carbon in the trees only, not the peat below, and come from a single project; the Indonesian water-table results are cited second-hand in a review [ev_wet_carbon_budi20_1, ev_wet_carbon_budi20_2, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_2].

justification.mechanism: Wetland management moderately increases carbon storage. Raising the water table on drained peat stops the stored carbon from rotting away, so carbon dioxide losses fall, even though methane rises. Rewetting drained farmland peat in Germany is estimated to save 20 to 35 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per hectare a year [ev_wet_carbon_meye26_1], and each 10 cm the water table is raised cuts net warming by at least 3 tonnes per hectare a year [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_1]. IPCC guidance adds that rewetting cuts waterborne carbon losses (a median 36% in the studies it collated) and that nitrous oxide falls practically to zero once the water table is within 20 cm of the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc13wl_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc13wl_3]. Restored forested wetlands on former US farmland were modelled to store 15.8 to 92.4 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per hectare every five years [ev_carbon_sequestration_jenk10_1], and in Canada active moss reintroduction restored carbon uptake on extracted peat [ev_carbon_sequestration_unepgpa22_2]. Field studies confirm that blocking ditches and canals raises the water table [ev_water_table_depth_hold04_1, ev_water_table_depth_page09_1, ev_water_table_depth_wils11db_1]. On burned peat in South Sumatra, planted native trees took up 11.3 tonnes of CO2 per hectare a year (Shorea balangeran) and 12.4 tonnes (Dyera polyphylla) in their wood [ev_wet_carbon_budi20_1, ev_wet_carbon_budi20_2]. Reviews of Indonesian peat projects report canal blocks raising the water table: by about 60 cm in the dry season 100 m from a block in Riau, by 70 cm within 170 m of a block at Sungai Tohor, and by a metre over 2420 ha where communities built 12 blocks [ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_2, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_4, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_3].
justification.conditionality: The class is moderate because the size rests on modelled results. Methane is the trade-off: where water stands above the peat surface, methane warming can outweigh the carbon dioxide saved for years [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_4], and restored wetlands can warm the climate for their first years to decades, with the switch to net cooling estimated at 57 to 299 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_4]. A meta-analysis found methane up 122.3% after restoration, with total emissions no higher than before [ev_carbon_sequestration_xu25_3]. Partial rewetting slows but does not stop peat loss [ev_carbon_sequestration_unepgpa22_4]. In a Kalimantan simulation, raising water levels gave only a small, not significant fall in carbon dioxide [ev_carbon_sequestration_page09_2], and planting on rewetted tropical peat has failed: seedlings did no better beside a dammed canal, and aerial seeding survived at about 2% [ev_establishment_survival_page09_6, ev_establishment_survival_pusp21_4]. Most evidence is temperate, boreal and high-income, and the benefit goes to the climate, not to the farmer. The South Sumatra tree figures count carbon in the trees only, not the peat below, and come from a single project; the Indonesian water-table results are cited second-hand in a review [ev_wet_carbon_budi20_1, ev_wet_carbon_budi20_2, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_2].

A planning model for Indonesian peatlands counts large avoided emissions from restoration, mostly from preventing peat decay and fire [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan22_2]. justification.mechanism: In upper-middle-income peatlands, mostly Indonesia and Malaysia, the evidence points to a carbon benefit of unstated size: rewetting slows subsidence and the peat decay behind it, and carbon dioxide from peat is lowest when the water table is near the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauhiainen16_1]. Canal blocking in Kalimantan raised the dry-season water table [ev_water_table_depth_page09_1]. A planning model for Indonesian peatlands counts large avoided emissions from restoration, mostly from preventing peat decay and fire [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan22_2], and a synthesis judges rewetting a better climate option than keeping peat drained [ev_carbon_sequestration_lup23_1]. On burned peat in South Sumatra, planted native trees took up 11.3 tonnes of CO2 per hectare a year (Shorea balangeran) and 12.4 tonnes (Dyera polyphylla) in their wood [ev_wet_carbon_budi20_1, ev_wet_carbon_budi20_2]. Reviews of Indonesian peat projects report canal blocks raising the water table: by about 60 cm in the dry season 100 m from a block in Riau, by 70 cm within 170 m of a block at Sungai Tohor, and by a metre over 2420 ha where communities built 12 blocks [ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_2, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_4, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_3].
justification.conditionality: The size is not stated because almost no unit weighs carbon dioxide against methane: most report a single gas, subsidence or national totals. In a Kalimantan simulation, raising water levels gave only a small, not significant fall in carbon dioxide [ev_carbon_sequestration_page09_2]; laboratory work suggests peat keeps decaying even when waterlogged [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauhiainen16_2]; and methane moved in opposite directions at paired sites [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_4]. The planning model assumes immediate restoration. Revegetation is unreliable: seedlings did no better beside a dammed canal, and aerial seeding survived at about 2% [ev_establishment_survival_page09_6, ev_establishment_survival_pusp21_4]. A measured net balance from a rewetted site in this income group would strengthen the row. The South Sumatra tree figures count carbon in the trees only, not the peat below, and come from a single project; the Indonesian water-table results are cited second-hand in a review [ev_wet_carbon_budi20_1, ev_wet_carbon_budi20_2, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_2].

effect_mechanism: Coastal wetlands (mangroves and salt marshes) are strong natural carbon sinks because they take up far more carbon dioxide than the methane they emit. A comparison of wetland types found mangroves and salt marshes were the only two that remained net carbon sinks, because of the limited methane generated in coastal wetlands compared with the scale of carbon-dioxide uptake [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_5]. A global meta-analysis of natural coastal wetlands found that converting them to other land uses increased their greenhouse-gas warming potential by 7.8 times for constructed wetlands, 22.3 times for cropland and 29.5 times for aquaculture ponds on average, implying a correspondingly large potential benefit from protecting or restoring the wetland instead of converting it [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan20_1].
conditionality: This class is built from a very small, specific evidence base, just two sources, both studying existing or converted coastal wetlands rather than restoration projects measured directly, so the strong_positive rating does not mean every restoration project will show this scale of gain. effect_mechanism: Creating a wetland builds a new carbon store from scratch. In created riverine basins in Ohio, organic matter in surface soils increased by approximately 1% per 3-year period over the decade after construction [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mits05_6], and nitrous oxide fluxes from marsh and edge plots were lower when those plots were inundated than when the same plots were exposed to air [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_9]. conditionality: The methane cost of putting water onto land sits in the same sources. effect_mechanism: Studies disagree on whether wetland management lowers or raises flood hazard. On the side of a reduction, wooded wetlands in particular increase flood storage, reduce flood peaks and increase peak travel time [ev_wetflA_acre_wooded_wetland], and a Ramsar briefing note states that wetland protection and restoration buffer communities by reducing wave damage and floods [ev_wet_flood_hazard_ramsar18_2]. On the side of an increase, the same review reports that even where the dominant result is to increase water storage within the wetland, the overall result may still be an increase in flood peaks at the catchment scale [ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment], and that a change of vegetation from wet meadows to shrubs and trees can double the size and depth of the inundated area for the same size of flood [ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up].
conditionality: What separates the two sides is scale and position: the reductions are storage and roughness effects on the flood peak passing through or below the wetland [ev_wetflA_acre_wooded_wetland, ev_wet_flood_hazard_ramsar18_2], while the increases arise at catchment scale, where an on-site storage gain need not add up to a downstream benefit [ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment], and locally, where the roughness that slows the flood raises water level and flooded area on the re-vegetated floodplain itself [ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up]. The influence of drain blocking on flood flows has been notoriously difficult to detect at the basin scale [ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_basin_null]; and during major catastrophic floods the whole basin may be saturated, so the presence or absence of wetlands, or their management, has no effect [ev_wetflA_acre_catastrophic_null]. None of the units is a measurement of a flood outcome in this scope: they are a single review pooling UK, US, Canadian, Irish and Zimbabwean settings and a global policy brief. Siting matters as much as the practice: whether a wetland intervention lowers flood hazard depends on where it sits in the catchment and how large the flood is.

Wet farming is generally not profitable on biomass sales alone, and income is hard to keep at the conventional level [ev_wet_econret_neud26_1, ev_wet_econret_temm26_4]. German farms rewetting grassland lost on average 35% of gross margin [ev_wet_hhinc_meye26_1], and US landowners restoring wetland earn from carbon and hunting only about 18% of farming returns [ev_economic_return_jenk10_5]. On the other side, thatching reed and directly sold buffalo products can pay [ev_wet_econret_neud26_2], German fen wet pastures with hardy breeds were profitable in all scenarios [ev_economic_return_tann22_4], and Australian cane farmers building lagoons had benefit-cost ratios of 0.8 to 1.5, higher when raised land could grow cane [ev_wet_eff_cann22_3].
justification.conditionality: Product and payment separate the sides: bulk biomass loses while niche products and payment-backed systems can pay [ev_wet_econret_neud26_1, ev_wet_econret_neud26_2]. The German wet-farming profits include agri-environment payments [ev_economic_return_tann22_4], and the Australian lagoons were subsidised [ev_wet_eff_cann22_3]. Society-level returns are held out of the class: Wicken Fen's benefit-cost ratio of 4.4 against 1.3 for farming, and US wetlands repaying public costs within a year, both count public benefits [ev_economic_return_rgwo25_1, ev_economic_return_jenk10_4]. effect_mechanism: Vegetation and wetland structures hold soil and sediment in place, and the result is clearest for coastal marsh. Against a degraded shore, salt-marsh planting enhances shoreline protection, which the meta-analysis measures as vertical accretion, elevation change, sediment deposition and shoreline change rates (effect size 0.61) (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_3). A meta-analysis of China's coastal wetland restoration (Liu et al.) found coastal stabilization - indicators such as vertical accretion rate - significantly improved in restored against degraded wetlands, by 19.7 % (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_1). In the restoration sub-practice, South Africa's Manalana wetland is the only case: rehabilitation structures halted the advance of erosion gullies that would otherwise have continued throughout the wetland and degraded the entire area (ev_erosion_hazard_bbr_1).
conditionality: The class is moderate, and its strength comes from the coastal units: it concerns shoreline protection and coastal stabilization against a degraded marsh or coast, not soil loss from fields. The 0.61 effect size is on a scale the source does not define (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_3); the Chinese figure is a pooled response ratio across restoration types that include building dikes as well as planting (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_1). The peatland evidence is a single runoff-volume unit, not an erosion measurement: at a blanket-peat restoration, the share of storm rainfall becoming storm discharge did not change at either restored site relative to the bare control (ev_wetflA_shut_runoffcoef_null), the paper concluding that restoration shifted the timing and peak of delivery rather than the volume - a null that says the peatland evidence here does not speak to erosion. The Manalana gully result is a programme narrative without a measurement, and it concerns gullies cutting through the wetland itself rather than soil loss from surrounding fields (ev_erosion_hazard_bbr_1). Sediment that a wetland traps from water flowing through it is a water-quality service, not prevention of landscape erosion, and those units vote in the water-quality row, not here. Nothing in the pool measures soil loss on farmland, and apart from the South African case all of it comes from high- and upper-middle-income coastal and upland settings.

effect_mechanism: Marsh vegetation attenuates waves and currents as water passes through the canopy, so suspended sediment settles, the bed accretes and surface elevation is maintained while lateral erosion of the shoreline is reduced. That mechanism is measured from both ends: inside existing marsh against adjacent unvegetated mudflat, where most paired studies reported increased accretion or surface elevation or reduced erosion and the pooled effect on shoreline stabilisation was positive (ev_erosion_hazard_shep11_3, ev_erosion_hazard_shep11_4); and in planted marsh, which improved shoreline protection against degraded wetland (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_3). effect_mechanism: Rewetting a cut-over peat site - raising the water table, filling or blocking ditches, mulching and transferring a moss layer - stabilises the water table and keeps the exposed peat saturated, so less nutrient and carbon load is flushed from the surface. Against the realistic do-nothing counterfactual of an abandoned extraction site, the loads leaving restored sites were lower (ev_nutrient_removal_rasa23_5). justification.conditionality: The class rests on a single source, and within it on a thin subgroup of the meta-analysis, so the size is not robust [ev_water_regulation_liu24_1]. The outcome is a hydrological-regulation indicator of the wetland itself, not water available to farmers or relief of water stress on surrounding land, and coastal water is often brackish. It is from the Chinese coast, upper-middle-income; a second independent source measuring water supply or groundwater for users near a restored coastal wetland would be needed before this transfers.

effect_mechanism: On peat, rewetting puts the water table back towards where the drain took it from. On an eroding English upland peatland, peat barriers built across gullies raised mean water tables significantly at every distance class, in the peat pans from 0.003 m below ground level to 0.064 m above it and in the vegetated haggs from 0.188 to 0.175 m below ground within 0.5 m of the pan edge [ev_wetflA_gatis_watertable]. On cutaway peat, the water-table level was successfully recovered by active restoration through ditch blocking and dam construction [ev_water_regulation_rasa23_6]. In tropical peat the same holds behind canal dams, reported in a review of Indonesian restoration techniques (Dohong et al.): the water table within the dammed sites in the SSI canal, Sebangau National Park, remained above the threshold level of 40 cm below the peat surface during the dry year 2006, while the unblocked control canal fell significantly below it (Panda et al. 2012) [ev_water_regulation_doh18_1], and the water table within the Kalampangan canals increased up to 151 cm following dam installation (Limin et al. 2007) [ev_water_regulation_doh18_2]. A basin-scale model of rewetting drained peat in the Neman basin (Stachowicz et al.) puts the extra water retained at 69 to 344 m3·ha−1, or 23.6–118 M m3 across the basin [ev_water_regulation_sta22_1].
conditionality: The meta-analytic near-ditch groundwater result now sits in the peatland catchment water yield row. The English rise is in the mean rather than the typical state: median water-table conditions remained similar at all distances after restoration, so the significant mean rise is driven by the wet tail [ev_wetflA_gatis_watertable]. Water-table fluctuation and the moisture dynamics of the peat layer were found difficult to maintain in restored peat-extraction areas, so the level returns but its dynamics do not [ev_water_regulation_rasa23_7]; and many hydrological processes do not fully recover within the first years after restoration, because degradation has already changed peat structure and consolidation, so early results are not the steady state and the monitoring windows behind most restoration claims are shorter than the recovery time [ev_wetflA_acre_recovery_timescale]. The Indonesian results are cited second-hand from single canal systems, a before-after rise and a dammed-against-unblocked comparison through a dry year [ev_water_regulation_doh18_1, ev_water_regulation_doh18_2]. The Neman model is a scenario estimate, and its basin total corresponds to 0.14–0.7% of the total annual Neman River discharge into the Baltic Sea - water held in the peat, not delivered to users [ev_water_regulation_sta22_1]. Apart from the Indonesian canal cases the units are temperate or boreal, from the UK, Ireland, Canada, Fennoscandia and northern Europe; none is from a low- or lower-middle-income setting, and none measures water available to a farming system or water stress experienced by farmers.

effect_mechanism: Wetlands store rain and release it slowly [ev_wet_water_regulation_ramsar18_1]. A meta-analysis finds wetlands on average support low flows [ev_water_regulation_kad16_1]. In Lao PDR a weir doubled the farmland able to use wetland water [ev_wgy_lao_1]; in Belarus managed water levels kept a fen close to its target [ev_wgy_blr_5]; and in Cameroon restored floods refilled waterholes, shortening the distance livestock walk to water [ev_water_access_deficit_loth04_3].
conditionality: The class is moderate. A global review of existing wetlands found headwater wetlands more often increase than reduce flow swings [ev_water_regulation_bull03_13]. Field studies found no significant gain in floodplain storage where models showed one [ev_wetflA_zhu_restoration_variability]. The Lao gain comes from a weir, the Belarus levels depend on ongoing regulation, and the Cameroon result is grey literature [ev_wgy_lao_1, ev_wgy_blr_5, ev_water_access_deficit_loth04_3].
